@graph.headline: What Is the Kelly Criterion in Trading? Formula & Examples
@graph.description: A 60% win rate at R=1.5 gives 33.33% full Kelly — ₹66,667 on ₹2,00,000. The formula, half and quarter Kelly, and how to turn Kelly % into shares, worked in ₹.

mainEntity.name: What is the Kelly criterion in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Kelly gives the fraction of your account to risk on each trade, from the strategy's own win rate and average win-to-loss ratio, to maximise long-run logarithmic growth for a repeated edge. Full Kelly is the theoretical maximum-growth fraction; in practice it is used as a ceiling, with fractional Kelly traded instead.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate the Kelly criterion?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use Kelly % = W − [(1 − W) ÷ R], where W is your win rate as a decimal and R is your average win divided by your average loss, both measured from your own closed trade history. For example, W = 0.60 and R = 1.5 gives 33.33% full Kelly — 16.67% at half Kelly, 8.33% at quarter Kelly — then multiply by account size for the rupee risk amount and divide by per-share stop distance for shares.

mainEntity.name: What is a good Kelly percentage for a retail trader?

acceptedAnswer.text: No one Kelly percentage counts as "good" for everyone. The survivable default is fractional Kelly — half or quarter of the full figure — combined with a fixed-risk cap, with the exact fraction set by how confident you are in your inputs and how much drawdown you can tolerate.

mainEntity.name: Why is full Kelly considered too risky?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three reasons: inputs are estimated from finite samples, so estimation error overstates the true edge and leads to over-betting; the single-bet formula does not size simultaneous or correlated positions; and full-Kelly swings are deep enough to break discipline before the mathematics pays off. Fractional Kelly directly addresses all three by cutting the stake, leaving room for input error, and producing a ride a trader can actually stay with.

mainEntity.name: What is half Kelly / fractional Kelly, and which fraction should I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fractional Kelly means trading a fraction of the full Kelly percentage — half Kelly trades 50% of f\, quarter Kelly trades 25% of f\. Half Kelly keeps about 75% of full Kelly's long-run growth at roughly half the volatility; quarter Kelly gives up more growth again, but at much lower drawdowns than half Kelly.

mainEntity.name: What does a negative Kelly percentage mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: A zero or negative Kelly result means the measured win rate and payoff ratio show no edge. Do not trade that system, and do not try to "size it anyway" — fix the strategy, test for a genuine edge on fresh data, or discard it.

mainEntity.name: How many trades do I need before I can trust my Kelly inputs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Same prescription as the input-discipline section: at least 50–100 trades from one consistent strategy before trusting the inputs, re-checked every 50–100 trades or quarterly. This is a recommended discipline, not a verified statistical threshold — even at 100 trades, a small sample still carries wide uncertainty.

mainEntity.name: Does the Kelly criterion work for options / intraday trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: The formula can be applied wherever a win rate and an average win and loss can be honestly measured from actual trade history, including intraday trading. But options expiry, gap risk, leverage, and changing volatility all break the tidy assumptions behind the formula — so fractional Kelly and a fixed-risk cap matter more for options and intraday trading, not less, and if the win rate and averages cannot be honestly measured, Kelly should not be used for it.

mainEntity.name: Kelly criterion vs fixed 2% risk — which is better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither wins in all cases: Kelly is better with a well-measured, stable edge; a fixed 2% rule is better when inputs are uncertain, trades are correlated, or regimes are changing. The strongest practical rule combines them: fractional Kelly as the ceiling, fixed risk as the cap, and the smaller rupee amount as the trade's risk.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert a Kelly percentage into a number of shares?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide the rupee risk amount by your per-share stop distance, and floor the result to whole shares — the worked example above does exactly this (₹16,667 ÷ ₹50 = 333 shares).
